3.3 Exact coverage in finite samples under the location-shift model

In Sections 3.1 and 3.2, we considered the limits as the sample size increases, in which the differences among H 1 (θ 0 ), . . . , H L (θ 0 ) are large relative to the standard errors of H l ( ˆ︁ θ). To examine the consequences of the construction of the intervals when these differences are comparable to the standard errors, we consider the location-shift model where p = 1, b l ∈ R and c > 0 are constants, σ > 0 is known, and ˆ︁ Σ = σ 2 .

In this model, the differences among the GCM-specific impacts do not depend on θ, and the coverage can be computed exactly. We examine the case in which these differences depend on the coefficients in the simulation study in Section 4. Under model (3.1), the coverage of I eCI (α) for µ L (θ 0 ) depends on the GCMs only through e l = {H l (θ 0 ) -µ L (θ 0 )}/(cσ) (l = 1, . . . , L). See Section S4.1 of the Supplementary Material for the expression of the coverage.

Figure 1(a) and (b) show the coverage of I eCI (α) for µ L (θ 0 ) with one GCM distant from the others, i.e., b1 = • • • = b L-1 = 0 and b L = cσβ. The coverage was at least 1 -α for every value of β if L ≤ 2/α. If L > 2/α, it was above 1 -α for small values of β but decreased for large values of β, e.g., to below 0.001 for L ∈ {41, 50} at 1 -α = 0.95 and β = 300. See Section S4.2 of the Supplementary Material for the coverage in other configurations.

For µ ∞ (θ 0 ), we consider the normal random-effects model, in which b 1 , . . . , b L in model (3.1) are independently distributed as N (b 0 , τ² ), and V = c 2 σ 2 . In Figure 1(c) with L = 3, the coverage of I µ (0.05) decreased as τ² /V increased, that of I eCI (0.05) was below 0.95 for τ² /V ≥ 2.37 and approximately 0.82 at τ² /V = 100, and that of I RE,t (0.05) was at least 0.966. See Section S4.3 of the Supplementary Material for the expressions of the coverage and the results with L ∈ {5, 10, 20}.

4 Simulation study

In the simulation study, we compared the coverage of the intervals in a setting that mimics projections of heat-related mortality, in which the impact is a nonlinear function of the coefficients, the differences among the GCM-specific impacts depend on the coefficients, and the coefficients are estimated by the quasi-likelihood method. We also compared the intervals for the mean over a population of GCMs and for the impact under a new GCM.

4.1 Data generation

We generated the daily mean temperature T i (i = 1, . . . , 3650) over 10 years by T i = 11.5 + 6.5 sin where d i = (i -1) mod 365, and υ 1 , υ 2 , . . . is the stationary first-order autoregressive process with the coefficient 0.75 and the marginal standard deviation 2.6, i.e., υ 1 ∼ N (0, 2.6 2 ) and )} ⊤ θ denote the log relative risk at the temperature T relative to the reference temperature 18, where B(T ) ∈ R 4 is the natural cubic spline basis with the knots at the 10th, 75th, and 90th percentiles and the boundary knots at the 0.1th and 99.9th percentiles of the temperature distribution.

We generated the daily number of deaths Y i independently given T i and ξ i by where D ∈ {20, 150} is the expected number of daily deaths at the reference temperature, and ξ 1 , ξ 2 , . . . are independently distributed as the gamma distribution with the shape 50 and the mean 1.

We set the true coefficient vector θ 0 so that the log relative risk f θ 0 (T ) is close to 0.0009(18 -T ) 2 for T < 18 and 0.0045(T -18) 2 for T ≥ 18, i.e., θ 0 is the value of θ with the smallest sum of the squared differences between f θ (T ) and this function at 1,000 equally spaced values of T between the boundary knots. See Section S5 of the Supplementary Material for the knots and the computation of the percentiles. For each GCM l, we generated the daily temperature over a future period of 21 years by T li = 11.5 + 6.5 sin where ∆ l is the warming of GCM l, which is amplified in summer, and υ l1 , υ l2 , . . . is generated independently in the same manner as υ 1 , υ 2 , . . ..

We defined the impact as the annual number of heat-attributable deaths

For the ensembles with the fixed GCMs, which we refer to as the fixed ensembles, we considered the following three designs, in which the GCM-specific temperature series were fixed across the repetitions. In the spread design, ∆ l = 2.5 + 0.8z (l-0.5)/L (l = 1, . . . , L) with L ∈ {3, 5, 10, 20, 50}, where z u denotes the u-quantile of the standard normal distribution.

In the hot-model design, ∆ l = 2.5 + 0.4z (l-0.5)/(L-1) (l = 1, . . . , L -1) and ∆ L = 6 with L ∈ {5, 10, 20, 50}, which represents an ensemble including a GCM with a high equilibrium climate sensitivity (Hausfather et al., 2022). In the large-ensemble design, ∆1 = • • • = ∆ L-1 = 2.5 and ∆ L = 6 with L ∈ {5, 10, 20, 50}, which represents an ensemble consisting of one other GCM and the members of an initial-condition large ensemble of one GCM (Deser et al., 2020). The members of the large ensemble differ only in the internal variability.

For the ensembles with the randomly sampled GCMs, which we refer to as the random ensembles, we generated a population of 1,000 GCMs with ∆ l drawn from N (2.5, 0.8 2 ), whose temperature series were fixed across the repetitions, and in each repetition, we sampled L ∈ {3, 5, 10, 20} GCMs and one new GCM with replacement from the population, so that the GCMs were sampled independently as in Section 3.2. The estimand µ ∞ (θ 0 ) is the mean of H l (θ 0 ) over the population.

4.2 Methods

We estimated θ by the quasi-likelihood method with the variance proportional to the mean and the mean model where κ 0 , κ 1k , κ 2k (k = 1, 2, 3), and κ 3m (m = 1, . . . , 6) are the nuisance parameters, and w im is 1 if (i -1) mod7 = m and 0 otherwise, which indicates the day of the week.

This mean model has the components of the models in time series studies of temperature and mortality (Bhaskaran et al., 2013), with the seasonality represented by the harmonic terms and without the lagged temperatures, in accordance with the data generation. We estimated the covariance matrix of 2026). We drew J = 1,000 coefficient vectors from N 4 ( ˆ︁ θ, ˆ︁ Σ) and computed the intervals at 1 -α ∈ {0.95, 0.90, 0.66}, for which L > 2/α holds for L = 50 at all levels and for L ≥ 10 at 1 -α = 0.66. We computed the empirical quantiles by the linear interpolation of type 7 of Hyndman and Fan (1996), which is the default in R and NumPy in Python.

For the fixed ensembles, we evaluated the coverage of I eCI (α) and I µ (α) for µ L (θ 0 ), the ratio of the median width of I eCI (α) to that of I µ (α), and the coverage of I eCI (α) for H s (θ 0 ). For the random ensembles, we evaluated the coverage of I eCI (α), I µ (α), I RE,t (α), and I RE,sim (α) for µ ∞ (θ 0 ) and the coverage of I eCI (α) and I new (α) for H new (θ 0 ). We repeated the data generation 2,000 times for each setting.

4.3 Results

Table 2 shows the coverage for the fixed ensembles with D = 150. See Section S5 of the Supplementary Material for the results with D = 20 and the coverage for H s (θ 0 ). The coverage of I µ (α) for µ L (θ 0 ) was close to the nominal level in all designs, between 0.960 and 0.962 at 1 -α = 0.95 and between 0.668 and 0.670 at 1 -α = 0.66. The coverage of I eCI (α) for H s (θ 0 ) was close to the nominal level with D = 150, between 0.950 and 0.955 at 1 -α = 0.95 and between 0.651 and 0.675 at 1 -α = 0.66, whereas with D = 20, it was below the nominal level in some settings, e.g., 0.627 at 1 -α = 0.66 for L = 5 in the large-ensemble design.

At 1 -α = 0.95, the coverage of I eCI (0.05) for µ L (θ 0 ) was close to one rather than the nominal level. Over the 26 settings with D ∈ {20, 150}, it was 1.000 in 10 settings and at least 0.99 in 22 settings, and with D = 150, the median width of I eCI (0.05) was 1.14 to 3.91 times that of I µ (0.05). This was also the case for L = 50 > 2/α, for which µ L (θ 0 ) was between the second smallest and the second largest of H 1 (θ 0 ), . . . , H L (θ 0 ) in all designs, i.e., the condition in Theorem 3.1(i) was satisfied. At 1 -α = 0.90, the coverage of I eCI (0.10) was at least the nominal level in all settings.

At 1 -α = 0.66, for which 2/α ≈ 5.9, the coverage of I eCI (0.34) with D = 150 decreased for L > 2/α in the designs including the GCM with ∆ L = 6. In the large-ensemble design, it was 0.963 for L = 5, whereas it was 0.537, 0.651, and 0.679 for L = 10, 20, and 50, respectively, of which only the coverage for L = 10 was below the nominal level by more than the Monte Carlo standard error. In the hot-model design, it was 0.960 for L = 5 and between 0.754 and 0.840 for L ≥ 10, and in the spread design, it was at least 0.936. With D = 20, for which the standard errors of H l ( ˆ︁ θ) are larger relative to the differences among the GCM-specific impacts, the coverage of I eCI (0.34) was at least 0.664 in all designs.

Table 3 shows the results for the random ensembles at 1 -α = 0.95. See Section S5 of the Supplementary Material for the results at 1 -α = 0.66. For µ ∞ (θ 0 ), the coverage of I RE,t (0.05) was at least 0.967 and that of I RE,sim (0.05) was between 0.946 and 0.953, whereas that of I µ (0.05) was between 0.769 and 0.938. The coverage of I eCI (0.05) was 0.947 and 0.924 for L = 3 with D = 20 and D = 150, respectively, and at least 0.976 for L ≥ 5. For H new (θ 0 ), the coverage of I eCI (0.05) was between 0.758 and 0.935, whereas that of I new (0.05) was at least 0.947. The median width of I RE,t (0.05) was approximately twice that of I eCI (0.05) for L = 3 and between 0.53 and 0.81 times for L ≥ 10.

Note that, with the 2,000 repetitions, the Monte Carlo standard error of the coverage is approximately 0.005 at 0.95 and 0.011 at 0.66. We reanalyzed the projections of heat-related mortality in London under SSP2-4.5 in the tutorial of Quijal-Zamorano et al. (2026). In the tutorial, the age-specific exposure-response functions for persons younger than 75 years and those aged 75 years or older were estimated by the quasi-likelihood method with the variance proportional to the mean, in which the mean of the daily number of deaths was modeled by a distributed lag nonlinear model (Gasparrini et al., 2010). The daily numbers of heat-attributable deaths from 1950 to 2099 were projected with the daily temperature trajectories of L = 3 GCMs and J = 100 coefficient draws. We used the daily attributable numbers of deaths at the point estimate and the coefficient draws for each GCM and each age group, which are available from the repository of the tutorial.

5.2 Methods

The target of the reported mean depends on the purpose of the projection. The mean µ L (θ 0 ) over the three GCMs is the target when the purpose is the projection under these GCMs, and the mean µ ∞ (θ 0 ) over a population of GCMs is the target when the three GCMs are regarded as a sample representing the differences among climate models. The eCI is the interval for H s (θ 0 ), the impact under one of the three GCMs selected uniformly at random.

For the two age groups and the total population, we computed the annual heat-attributable deaths in each decade and in two 21-year periods, the GCM-specific window centered on the year in which the global warming level of 2 • C is reached and the period 2079-2099. For each of them, we computed ˆ︁ µ, I eCI (α), I µ (α), and I RE,t (α) at 1 -α ∈ {0.95, 0.66}, where the empirical quantiles were computed as in Section 4.2. The values of ˆ︁ µ and I eCI (0.05) agreed with those reported in the tutorial. For the two 21-year periods, we estimated the Monte Carlo standard errors of the endpoints of the intervals by the standard deviations over 2,000 resamples of the J coefficient draws with replacement, in which the impacts under the GCMs with the same draw were resampled together. For the two 21-year periods, we also computed H l ( ˆ︁ θ) and the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of H l (θ (j) ) over the draws for each GCM, and we decomposed the variance of the pooled impacts H l (θ (j) ) (l = 1, . . . , L; j = 1, . . . , J), from which the quantiles in I eCI (α) are computed, into the mean of the variances over the draws within the GCMs and the variance of the means over the draws among the GCMs, which is analogous to the partition of the uncertainty in climate predictions into its sources (Hawkins and Sutton, 2009).

5.3 Results

Figure 2 and Table 4 show the results. At 1 -α = 0.95, the difference in the widths of I eCI (0.05) and I µ (0.05) increased in later decades, particularly for persons aged 75 years or older and the total population. For the total population, I eCI (0.05) and I µ (0.05) were (906, 1883) and (1060, 1520) for the 2 • C warming level and (906, 3033) and (1434, 2061) for 2079-2099, respectively. For persons aged 75 years or older and the total population, the differences between the corresponding endpoints of I eCI (0.05) and I µ (0.05) in the two 21-year periods were at least 4.8 times the larger of the Monte Carlo standard errors of the two endpoints. For persons younger than 75 years, the differences between the lower limits were less than twice the Monte Carlo standard errors, so that the comparison of these endpoints is not reliable with J = 100.

For 2079-2099, H l ( ˆ︁ θ) for the total population was 2714, 1478, and 1063 under ACCESS-CM2, BCC-CSM2-MR, and CESM2, respectively, and the percentile interval for ACCESS-CM2, (2247, 3175), did not overlap with those for BCC-CSM2-MR and CESM2, (1189, 1756) and (866, 1254). The variance among the GCMs accounted for 94% of the variance of the pooled impacts for 2079-2099 and 82% for the 2 • C warming level. See Section S6 of the Supplementary Material for the results for each GCM and each age group. For 2079-2099, the upper and lower limits of I eCI (0.05) were determined only by the draws under ACCESS-CM2 and CESM2, respectively. Thus, the upper limit 3033 of I eCI (0.05) represents the burden under the GCM with the largest impact rather than the uncertainty in the mean over the three GCMs, for which the upper limit of I µ (0.05) was 2061.

Since L = 3 < 2/α for both levels, the coverage of I eCI (α) for µ L (θ 0 ) converges to 1 by Theorem 3.1(i) unless the GCM-specific impacts are all equal. However, the standard deviations of H l (θ (j) ) over the draws for the total population ranged from 101 to 152 for the 2 • C warming level and from 104 to 247 for 2079-2099 among the three GCMs, so that the differences among the GCM-specific impacts depend on the coefficients, and the coverage for the sample size of these data is not guaranteed by the theorem.

For µ ∞ (θ 0 ), I RE,t (0.05) was (349, 2253) and (-500, 4004) for the total population, which were wider than I eCI (0.05) because of the quantile t 2,0.975 = 4.30. The negative lower limit for 2079-2099 is due to the normal distribution of the GCM-specific impacts assumed in I RE,t (α) with L = 3. In the tutorial, the attributable fraction (RR -1)/RR on the days above the minimum mortality temperature was not truncated at 0, where RR is the relative risk, so that the nonnegativity of µ ∞ (θ 0 ) does not follow from the definition of the impacts. At 1 -α = 0.66, I RE,t (0.34) was (1026, 1576) and (1101, 2402), which were narrower than I eCI (0.34), (1030, 1645) and (1051, 2674). For the total population, the Monte Carlo standard errors of the endpoints of I eCI (α), I µ (α), and I RE,t (α) were at most 62 at both levels.

6 Discussion

In this study, we specified the targets for which the GCM-ensemble mean is reported and the intervals aligned with them. The eCI used in previous studies is aligned with the impact under a GCM selected uniformly at random from the considered set. Its nominal level does not indicate its coverage for the mean over the considered GCMs or for the mean over a population of GCMs. Table S1 of the Supplementary Material summarizes the coverage of the intervals for their targets and that of the eCI for the other targets, obtained in Sections 3 and 4.

The appropriate target depends on the purpose of each study. For example, when the purpose is the projection under the considered GCMs, the target is µ L (θ 0 ), and I µ (α) is the interval aligned with this target. Since I µ (α) does not represent the differences among the GCMs, these differences can be shown separately by the GCM-specific impacts, e.g., H l ( ˆ︁ θ) with their percentile intervals as in Table S6 of the Supplementary Material. The eCI can also be useful to represent these differences, but its nominal level does not indicate its coverage probability for µ L (θ 0 ), so that it should be interpreted separately from I µ (α), the asymptotic confidence interval for µ L (θ 0 ). Note that, since I µ (α) is computed from the same coefficient draws as the eCI, it can be obtained in existing projections without additional computation.

The targets can also be related to the impact under the actual climate, depending on how the GCMs are related to the actual climate. Annan and Hargreaves (2010) contrasted two paradigms for interpreting multi-model ensembles in climate science. In the truth-centred paradigm, the GCMs are regarded as sampled from a distribution centered on the actual climate. If this centering also holds for the impacts, the impact under the actual climate corresponds to µ ∞ (θ 0 ). In the paradigm of a statistically indistinguishable ensemble, the actual climate is regarded as exchangeable with the GCMs. If the GCMs and the actual climate are regarded as independent draws from the same population, the impact under the actual climate corresponds to H new (θ 0 ). If the actual climate is regarded as one of the considered GCMs, each with the probability 1/L, the impact under the actual climate corresponds to H s (θ 0 ). In practice, however, the GCMs in multi-model ensembles share components and code, and some GCMs are near-replicates of others (Knutti et al., 2013; Abramowitz et al., 2019), so that the effective number of independent GCMs may be smaller than L, and the population of GCMs over which µ ∞ (θ 0 ) is defined may not be specified in practice (Tebaldi and Knutti, 2007).

To our knowledge, the terminology "empirical confidence interval" in this literature dates at least to Gasparrini and Leone (2014). In their setting, the coefficients were drawn from an approximate sampling distribution and mapped through the same attributable-risk functional as the point estimate, and the empirical percentiles can be interpreted as a simulation-based approximate confidence interval for the attributable risk. In the GCM ensemble, the pooling across the GCMs changes the functional through which the coefficient draws are mapped, and the interpretation of the empirical percentiles changes accordingly.

In large samples with the GCMs fixed, whether the eCI covers µ L (θ 0 ) depends on L relative to 2/α. At 1 -α = 0.95, L < 40 holds in the projection studies that reported the eCI with 5 (Guo et al., 2018), 18 (Chen et al., 2024 ), 27 (Zhan et al., 2023), and 28 (Yang et al., 2021) GCMs, for which the eCI is conservative for the mean over the considered GCMs unless the GCM-specific impacts are all equal, and its coverage was close to one in the simulation study. In contrast, Weinberger et al. (2017) pooled 41 and 42 simulation runs of 20 GCMs under the two emission scenarios, including 10 runs of one GCM, for which L > 2/α at 1 -α = 0.95, and the coverage converges to 0 if the impact under one GCM is so large that µ L (θ 0 ) exceeds the second largest of H 1 (θ 0 ), . . . , H L (θ 0 ). For lower nominal levels, the condition L < 2/α is more restrictive, i.e., L < 20 for 1 -α = 0.90 and L ≤ 5 for 1 -α = 0.66, and the coverage was 0.537 at 1 -α = 0.66 for L = 10 in the large-ensemble design in the simulation study.

When the GCMs are regarded as a sample from a population with normally distributed impacts, the coverage of I µ (α) for the population mean converges to 0, since I µ (α) does not account for the sampling of the GCMs, and if L < 2/α, that of the eCI converges to 1 -2 1-L . In contrast, I RE,t (α) accounts for both the estimation of the coefficients and the sampling of the GCMs, although it is wide for a small number of GCMs because of the quantile of the t distribution with L -1 degrees of freedom, as in the reanalysis with L = 3.

This study has the following limitations. With a small number of coefficient draws, the endpoints of the intervals are subject to Monte Carlo error, which was small relative to the differences between the intervals for the total population in the reanalysis with J = 100. The coverage of I µ (α) for µ L (θ 0 ) relies on the consistency of n ˆ︁ Σ for Σ 0 in Assumption 1, which may not hold for the estimator in Section 4.2 if the conditional variance of the daily number of deaths given the covariates is not proportional to the conditional mean. In such cases, a sandwich estimator can be used for ˆ︁ Σ without changing the construction of the intervals. The intervals for µ ∞ (θ 0 ) assume that the GCMs are sampled independently from a population. We did not consider other sources of uncertainty, such as the bias correction of the GCM outputs, the internal variability of the climate, and the demographic scenarios.

Disclosure

Generative artificial intelligence tools (ChatGPT 5.6 Sol, ChatGPT 6.1 Terra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro) were used to assist with language editing and code drafting. The author reviewed and verified the final code and text and takes responsibility for the content.

S5.1 Data generation and computation

The coefficient vector θ 0 was computed by least squares on 1,000 equally spaced temperatures between the boundary knots. The knots of the natural cubic spline basis were the percentiles of a temperature series of 500 years generated in the same manner as the observed temperature, and they were -1.38, 4.55, 15.75, 18.41, and 24.34. The basis was computed for the scaled temperature (T -15)/10, and it is linear below the lower boundary knot and above the upper boundary knot. In the computation of H l (θ), we rounded the temperature down to bins of width 0.1 • C and evaluated f θ at the midpoints of the bins, and H l (θ 0 ) was computed in the same manner. In the large-ensemble design, the L -1 members with ∆ l = 2.5 had temperature series generated independently, so that the members differ only in the internal variability.

S5.2 Additional results

Tables S3-S5 show the coverage for the fixed ensembles with D = 20, the coverage of I eCI (α) for H s (θ 0 ), and the results for the random ensembles at 1 -α = 0.66. With D = 20, the coverage of I µ (α) was between 0.941 and 0.944 at 1 -α = 0.95 and between 0.660 and 0.664 at 1 -α = 0.66. For the random ensembles at 1 -α = 0.66, the coverage for µ ∞ (θ 0 ) was at least 0.676 for I RE,t (0.34), between 0.659 and 0.699 for I RE,sim (0.34), between 0.704 and 0.922 for I eCI (0.34), and between 0.453 and 0.644 for I µ (0.34), and the coverage for H new (θ 0 ) was between 0.539 and 0.661 for I eCI (0.34) and at least 0.680 for I new (0.34).
